query: For refractory high-entropy alloys intended for structural use under extreme-temperature conditions, what single intervention could improve high-temperature oxygen resistance? State one hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains its mechanism, predicts the improvement relative to the untreated alloy, defines the temperature, atmosphere, and exposure conditions under which it should work, cites supporting prior evidence, and proposes an experiment with a clear result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.target_system: Refractory high-entropy alloys for structural use under extreme-temperature conditions

evidence_appraisal.reason: The record discusses the formation of carbide with the concentration of carbon in a specific RHEA, which may provide insights into improving high-temperature oxygen resistance, but the composition is different from the target system.

evidence_appraisal.difference_from_target: Composition and focus on mechanical properties
evidence_appraisal.reason: The record examines the evolution of microstructure and mechanical properties of a specific RHEA upon aging at 700°C, which may provide some insights into the behavior of RHEAs at high temperatures, but the focus is on mechanical properties rather than oxygen resistance.
The record discusses property goals for new ultra-high temperature alloys, including oxidation resistance, but it is a broader class of materials than RHEAs.

generation.hypothesis: The addition of a small amount of carbon (around 0.1 at.%) to refractory high-entropy alloys can improve their high-temperature oxygen resistance by forming stable carbides, such as Ta3C and Nb3C, which can act as a barrier against oxygen diffusion.
generation.material_initial_state: As-cast or homogenized refractory high-entropy alloys
generation.intervention: Addition of a small amount of carbon (around 0.1 at.%)
generation.structural_mediator: Formation of stable carbides, such as Ta3C and Nb3C
generation.mechanism: The formation of stable carbides can act as a barrier against oxygen diffusion, reducing the oxidation rate of the alloy. This mechanism is derived from materials-science principles and supported by the partial transfer of record PMC7517255::web::000::abstract.
generation.predicted_outcome: Improved high-temperature oxygen resistance, with a potential reduction in oxidation rate of at least 20% compared to the untreated alloy
generation.boundary: The improvement in oxygen resistance is expected to be significant at high temperatures (above 800°C) and high pressures (above 6 GPa), but may be less pronounced at lower temperatures and pressures
generation.uncertainty: The exact amount of carbon required to achieve the optimal improvement in oxygen resistance is uncertain and may depend on the specific composition of the alloy

falsification_experiment.design: Expose samples of refractory high-entropy alloys with and without the addition of carbon to high-temperature (above 800°C) and high-pressure (above 6 GPa) conditions for an extended period (at least 100 hours) and measure the oxidation rate
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the oxidation rate of the alloy with the addition of carbon is not significantly lower (at least 20% reduction) than the untreated alloy, the hypothesis is falsified

cited_evidence.text: In this work, the formation of carbide with the concertation of carbon at 0.1 at.% in refractory high-entropy alloy (RHEA) Mo15Nb20Re15Ta30W20 was studied under both ambient and high-pressure high-temperature conditions. The x-ray diffraction of dilute carbon (C)-doped RHEA under ambient pressure showed that the phases and lattice constant of RHEA were not influenced by the addition of 0.1 at.% C. In contrast, C-doped RHEA showed unexpected phase formation and transformation under combined high-pressure and high-temperature conditions by resistively employing the heated diamond anvil cell (DAC) technique. The new FCC_L12 phase appeared at 6 GPa and 809 °C and preserved the ambient temperature and pressure. High-pressure and high-temperature promoted the formation of carbides Ta3C and Nb3C, which are stable and may further improve the mechanical performance of the dilute C-doped alloy Mo15Nb20Re15Ta30W20.
